newsitem.title: UK: Treasuries higher in London, calm ahead of data.
newsitem.headline: Treasuries higher in London, calm ahead of data.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries inched higher in subdued London trading on Wednesday after the boost from Greenspan's reassuring comments left the market anticipating only a slight ripple from U.S. data due later, analysts said.
"It's marking time, but is looking to go up," said Nick Benton, a trader at Bank America in London, "having pushed up strongly yesterday, on the back of Greenspan's comments.

Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan's upbeat report on the U.S. economy on Tuesday injected a positive tone into the market and triggered many players to cover their short positions, analysts said.
On the back of overnight rallies, the 30-year benchmark Treasury bond was up at 96-17 at 1100 GMT, yielding 6.773, after closing at 96-11 in Tokyo and New York.
Benton said after earlier profit-taking in Tokyo, there was reasonable two-way flow in London, with some European buying.
Dealers said U.S. December housing starts, due at 1330 GMT, and the Fed's Beige book due 1900 GMT, could cause a hiccup.
Don Smith, international economist at HSBC Markets in London, said trading would stay mediocre until the U.S. market opened.
"But then housing starts may have a bit of a negative effect," he said.
Smith said the strength of the housing market, reflected in most market indicators, suggested the recent rise was unlikely to be a short-term phenomenon that would be sharply reversed.
"The market is looking for what the Beige book will say about the interaction of the labour market with inflation and also how strong it thinks labour pressures are on inflation," he said.
But Benton said he expected the figures to have less effect than was expected prior to Greenspan's speech, which economists said indicated few signs of imbalances or inflationary tensions.
"I don't think (the data) will have enough imput to turn this market into being very negative," he said.
"The indications were (Greenspan) thinks inflation is well under control, and he's more focused on helping the United States reduce the deficit by allowing growth," said Benton.
At the short end, two-year U.S. notes were trading at 99-20, yielding 5.955 percent, unchanged from Tokyo and New York.
Dealers expected Wednesday's auction of $17.5 billion of two-year Treasuries to be easily absorbed.
"Given that everyone is very long in dollars at the moment, I think the two-year bond will find reasonable support," said Benton. "I certainly don't think people are quite as bearish as they were."
March T-bond futures were up slightly at 111-21 in automated trade, up 5/32 from Tuesday's Chicago settlement.
